latest_nl_proof:
Let H_m denote the harmonic number H_m = sum_{r=1}^m 1/r. We compute

sum_{j=1}^{n-1} H_{n-j}.

Make the substitution i = n-j. As j runs from 1 to n-1, i runs from n-1 down to 1, so

sum_{j=1}^{n-1} H_{n-j} = sum_{i=1}^{n-1} H_i.

Now expand each H_i:

sum_{i=1}^{n-1} H_i = sum_{i=1}^{n-1} sum_{r=1}^i 1/r.

Swap the order of summation. For a fixed r with 1 <= r <= n-1, the term 1/r appears once for each i with r <= i <= n-1, i.e. exactly n-r times. Hence

sum_{i=1}^{n-1} sum_{r=1}^i 1/r = sum_{r=1}^{n-1} (n-r)/r.

Therefore

sum_{j=1}^{n-1} H_{n-j} = sum_{r=1}^{n-1} (n-r)/r = n sum_{r=1}^{n-1} 1/r - sum_{r=1}^{n-1} 1
= nH_{n-1} - (n-1).

Finally, since H_n = H_{n-1} + 1/n, we have

n(H_n - 1) = n(H_{n-1} + 1/n - 1) = nH_{n-1} - (n-1).

Thus sum_{j=1}^{n-1} H_{n-j} = n(H_n - 1), as claimed.
